summary:
Allwork.Space reports that coworking and flexible office operators are adding gyms, fitness classes and wellness amenities as a competitive differentiator in a hybrid-work market reshaped by the pandemic. Examples cited via JLL include Monday Rio in Madrid, The Address in India and The Ministry in London.

Demand context: industry research cited by JLL found nearly a third of companies now use flexible office space, and more than 40% plan to increase that investment, driven by a desire to cut real estate costs while still offering employee perks. The flexible office market is projected to nearly triple from roughly $35 billion in 2023 to almost $97 billion by 2030.

On worker preferences, JLL data indicates most workers now prioritize work-life balance over salary, and remote employees are more likely than office-based workers to exercise during work hours. With hybrid workers averaging just over three office days per week, on-site gyms remove the need for a separate trip to a fitness club and bake fitness into the workday.

The employer case rests on productivity and health outcomes. A study in the International Journal of Workplace Health Management linked daytime exercise to improved mood, focus and stress resilience rather than midday fatigue. U.S. coworking chain Life Time reported that frequent gym users among its members required emergency or clinical care far less often than infrequent exercisers.

Industry voices position office gyms as part of a broader talent strategy, especially for attracting younger employees who treat wellness perks as standard. Supporters argue the amenity does double duty: lifting morale and retention while helping justify the return on investment in physical office space and, implicitly, supporting attendance in hybrid arrangements.

Remote employees are more likely than office-based employees to exercise during work hours
Hybrid workers average just over three office days per week
